The gold-to-silver ratio widened to 67.95 this morning, from 66.59 yesterday — giving back three sessions' worth of narrowing in one.

Kitco's live board read gold $4,384.10 and silver $64.52 at 06:00 New York time, both checked against TradingEconomics before this desk's tape moved. Measured against yesterday's mark, gold is down 0.70% and silver down 2.68% — more than triple the metal's move. The ratio ran 68.41 on 9 August, 67.84, 67.49, 66.59, and now 67.95: silver gave back in one session what it took across three.

Platinum and palladium were held for a second straight morning. Kitco read platinum $1,717.00, but two independent boards agreed with each other to within 50 cents and put Kitco $14.60 low — so the outlier is this paper's own board, not the market, and the earlier $1,710.00 mark stands under the one-price rule.

Silver is still up 1.67% on the week even after today's pullback, and gold is up 5.43% on 5 August. A workshop that repriced silver stock yesterday isn't wrong today — just less right.

India's largest branded jeweller has put a view on natural-diamond pricing on the record — and it's the first time in this paper's archive that the counter, not the index, has said it.

Ajoy Chawla, Titan's managing director, told an earnings call: "I think at the market level, it has stabilized," adding that the lab-grown-versus-natural argument has faded from the conversation. The quarter behind the remark is large: consolidated income of Rs 20,753 crore, up 40%; the jewellery division alone took Rs 18,253 crore, up 43% excluding bullion and digital gold, at a 12.9% margin. The group added 77 net stores to reach 3,680.

Everything this paper has published on polished pricing this month has come from the index end — RapNet's one-carat reading flat in July, the colour split inside it. Titan is describing what customers did at roughly 3,680 counters. When a supply-side index and a demand-side retailer stop disagreeing about direction in the same fortnight, the reading is firmer than either alone.

The limits are real: Titan sells natural diamonds and has been careful about lab-grown, so "stabilised" is a claim made by an interested party in the same week it reported a 43% jewellery quarter. Stabilised is also not the same word as recovered.

The sharpest thing said about polished prices this week didn't come from an index — it came from the cutting floor.

Senil Lakhani, president of Kiran Gems USA, told Rapaport's Heard on the Street that diamonds from 0.30 to 1.5 carats are "less expensive than ever before," selling at 1990s and early-2000s prices. He named the sizes that matter — 0.30, 0.40, 0.50 and 0.70 carats — "the bread and butter for America," priced between $1,000 and $5,000.

This paper has reported the same goods from the other end all month: 0.30-carat goods up 1.6% in July, 0.50-carat up 1.8%, against a flat one-carat. Those are monthly moves. Lakhani is describing where the price sits, not which way it's going — and a 1.6% month on a price sitting at a 1999 level is a small repair on a long decline.

No index this desk can reach publishes a 1999 comparison for these sizes, so the level claim can't be checked against a price history. What can be checked is direction, and direction agrees with him. It comes from a manufacturer, the part of the chain with the least to gain from calling polished cheap.
